#2018. West Ham Ticket Row: A Bit Of Pettiness? I’m All For It

West Ham United’s ticketing arrangements for the forthcoming Championship clash with Bristol City have caused controversy, but I have to say I’m firmly on the Hammers’ side with this one. If there’s an element of tit for tat involved, I don’t have a problem with it at all.

Bristol City supporters might not particularly like the situation, but there is some history between the two clubs when it comes to ticket allocations. During the FA Cup meeting in January 2024, Bristol City took their full allocation of around 9,000 tickets at the London Stadium, resulting in thousands of West Ham season-ticket holders having to move from their usual seats.

That caused considerable frustration at the time, with the West Ham United Supporters’ Trust seeking clarification from the club over the arrangements. So if the current situation feels like a bit of payback, I can certainly understand why.

One thing West Ham’s relegation to the Championship has provided is a real reality check when it comes to the treatment of travelling supporters.

In the Premier League, there was at least some collective understanding that away supporters shouldn’t be completely fleeced. The Football Supporters’ Federation’s original Twenty’s Plenty campaign eventually helped bring about the £30 away-ticket cap, which has remained in place since 2016.

It wasn’t perfect, and £30 was still more than supporters had originally campaigned for, but at least there was a limit.

That protection doesn’t exist across the Championship, and we’re now seeing the difference.

Take West Ham’s trip to Birmingham City in December, for example. According to the club’s official ticket information, adult supporters will be charged £37.50 for the privilege of watching the Hammers at St Andrew’s.

And it definitely feels like Championship clubs are treating us like absolute mugs.

When West Ham roll into town, we’re seen as a cash cow. Clubs know we’re going to bring a substantial travelling support, and it increasingly feels as though they’re happy to make the most of it.

Of course, I understand that Championship clubs have their own financial pressures, but that doesn’t make it any easier for supporters who are already spending a fortune travelling around the country.

I don’t have a problem with West Ham looking after our own fans, even if that means upsetting a few visiting supporters along the way.

Perhaps there’s a little bit of pettiness involved, but realistically, I don’t mind that either.

We’re West Ham, and the club should be looking after our fans. That ought to be the priority, particularly when supporters have been asked to put up with so much since dropping into the Championship.

And any Bristol City fans who don’t like it probably should look at their own club’s conduct when we played them in the FA Cup.

I don’t particularly want to see football clubs getting into an endless argument over ticket allocations, and ultimately I’d prefer supporters everywhere to be treated fairly.

But when it comes to this particular situation, I’m not going to criticise the West Ham hierarchy for giving a bit back.

Sometimes tit for tat is exactly what it looks like, and on this occasion, I’m perfectly happy with it.

Kris Gonzo (commonly known to the West Ham community as Gonzo) is the co-founder of Hammers Chat (established 2014) and the lead video content creator and columnist for Claret and Hugh.

With over a decade of professional sports media experience, he is a frequent West Ham United analyst and contributor for Sky Sports News, BBC Football Focus, and BBC Radio 5 Live. He previously served as an official video and content creator for West Ham United FC during the club's tenure at Upton Park and featured in the official documentary commemorating the historic final game at the Boleyn Ground.

A lifelong Hammer since the legendary 10-0 victory over Bury, when he isn't providing daily match analysis on the Hammers Chat YouTube Channel or broadcasting on X (@GONZObignose), he can be found walking his dog and restoring classic pinball machines.

Gonzo. So unlike you. I am also left bewildered at exactly what the tit for tat is all about. Could I respectfully suggest a follow up to explain what it is all about. Ken

Gonzo, I dont think at any point actually say what the club has done. You dont appear to explain what the pettiness is around, or even what it is we are doing? You said I’m not going to criticise the West Ham hierarchy for giving a bit back. So what bit is it they are giving back? You have gone all round the houses with everything else, but left the part about how the club is getting its own back completely void of details….so if Bristol City dont like it….like what exactly? lol

I thought I was being thick but I too couldn’t make out the point bring made in that article.

Wow i didn’t realise away supporters weren’t getting the sane compulsory pricing in the Champs, I used to love away games much better atmosphere and experience.

Next season if we don’t go up which is a possibility the chairman should speak to all the other clubs and arrange a reciprocal agreement, we will charge your fans what you charge ours.

#2017. West Ham’s £70k a week transfer blunder laid bare by damning statistic

Of the sixteen players who departed West Ham United  following relegation, some were sold, some were loaned out and some, like Callum Wilson, simply came to the end of their contracts and politely declined another, less lucrative deal to stay with the club as it slipped down into the Championship.

Wilson is now plying his trade at Brentford: Alongside him (admittedly, not often) in West Ham’s attack for the second half of last season was Adama Traore whose most memorable contribution was to throw Marc Cucurella to the ground and begin the fracas with Chelsea that saw Jean Clair Todibo red carded.

Traore was one of West Ham’s less effective signings last winter

Sadly Traore didn’t register a single goal during his stay at West Ham – in fact this is something of a wider issue for the bulked up attacker: According to the72.co.uk, Traore hasn’t scored a goal now for nearly two years:

Quite what made Nuno Espírito Santo so single minded in his demand for Traore at West Ham who can say: The winger might actually have been useful this season but he hopped off to Deportivo La Coruña where his goal less streak has continued rather than take the drop in league and salary.

Nice work if you can get it: A reported £70k a week at West Ham demonstrates fully pretty much everything that was wrong with the club’s recruitment: That’s the equivalent of over 3.5 million a year, for a player who contributed so little to the club’s survival effort. We wish him well.

#2015. “I don’t know why…” – John Aldridge fears Liverpool’s stance on one player could ‘backfire’

John Aldridge has questioned why Liverpool weren’t more assertive in pulling Dominik Szoboszlai out of national team duty when he’s currently nursing a minor injury.

The midfielder sprained his ankle in the 3-1 victory at Crystal Palace on Sunday, with Andoni Iraola uncertain after the game as to whether or not the 26-year-old would join up with his country during this international window.

In a statement on Tuesday, the Hungarian FA said that a decision on the player’s participation against Georgia and Northern Ireland over the next week will be deferred until the ‘last minute’ as his fitness continues to be assessed.

In his latest column for the Liverpool Echo, Aldridge voiced his belief that Liverpool should’ve done more to prevent Szoboszlai from playing for Hungary in the coming days when he’s clearly not fully fit.

The former Reds striker wrote: ‘I know Virgil van Dijk has pulled out of the Netherlands squad because of a little niggle, but Dominik Szoboszlai has stayed with Hungary despite injuring his knee against Palace.

‘Any other club would pull them out of international duty. Manchester United, Arsenal, Man City – they’d all pull them. We’ve seen it before. Any doubt and that’s it, decision made, you’re not playing. I don’t understand why we don’t throw our weight around like that.

‘I understand players want to play for their country. I was the same with Ireland. I would answer call-ups even when I was injured. I get what it means and how much it means to players, but any other club would just pull them. That’s not happened here, I don’t know why. Hopefully that just means it’s not that serious.

‘It still sounds like they’re taking a risk. If he stays with Hungary and plays, we’ve just got to hope the decision doesn’t backfire and come back to hurt Liverpool.’

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

As Szoboszlai is contracted to Liverpool, the Merseyside club could’ve blocked him from representing his country during this international window because of his knee injury.

However, it’d appear to be a case of the player wanting to at least link up with the Hungary camp and try to prove his fitness, and Anfield chiefs green-lighting that action out of respect for the 26-year-old and not wanting to antagonise him by forbidding him to travel.

The grey area over the midfielder potentially being fit enough to play but not certain of doing so has presented a tricky dilemma, as much as Iraola would no doubt have preferred for our number 8 to swerve national team duty and prioritise his club instead.

With Hungary not playing until Saturday, that does give Szoboszlai a bit of time to recover from the knee issue he incurred at Selhurst Park, and we’d like to think that Marco Rossi wouldn’t risk fielding him against Georgia unless he’s definitely OK to feature.

While a swift return to action for the 26-year-old would obviously be a good thing, we just hope it doesn’t come at the expense of his involvement for Liverpool in the coming weeks, especially with a hectic run of 11 matches in 40 days before the end of December.

Welcome to our Live Comments section, where new comments will appear automatically

It is all very well and good for pundits (code word for writers with preposterous assertions) to voice the opinion that LFC should have been more assertive in voicing their opinion on Szoboszlai not starting for Hungary. The problem with that line of thinking is that Szobo is always passionate to play for his country (and as seen last year in his performances to play for LFC), so if you deny him the right to play, you run the risk of alienating him, something Aldridge does not have to concern himself with because he has nothing to do with LFC or Szobo. I also worry that if he is allowed to start when not fit he will further injure himself, but believe Szobo and his manager will not take that action if he is not fit and can understand that Szobo as his country’s captain, if he does not start he would at least like to be on the sidelines giving his teammates moral support – something Aldridge also does not have to concern himself with! YNWA

#2012. Arteta named as by far the worst nightmare manager to deal with by former top referee

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Mikel Arteta has been named as by a distance the worst manager to deal with by a former top referee.

Zero surprise to anybody that the Arsenal boss has been named and shamed.

The embarrassing antics of Mikel Arteta on the touchline are there for all to see, as well as his behaviour in interviews and press conferences.

Never mind what he whispers in the ear and we can’t hear, as well as behind closed doors.

The naming and shaming of Mikel Arteta comes from former top Premier League referee Graham Scott.

He was speaking on the Athletic FC podcast in a conversation with Emma Paton, Dan Kilpatrick and Tim Spiers.

Emma Paton asking Graham Scott: “Who was the worst manager to deal with on the touchline?”

The former Premier League referee replying: “Well, the trite answer is: all of them when they’re losing. The honest answer, I’m afraid, I know whatever I say at this point just gets me pelters, but it is Mikel Arteta. He is the hardest work. He really does push all the limits all of the time. I don’t mind that in many ways; he’s trying to get a competitive advantage for his team. That’s fine. That’s part of his job. And of course, he’s entitled to do it, and it’s for us to place them, but he does make your life extremely difficult.”

Graham Scott going on to explain: “He’s out of his box (technical area) all the time. I watched him recently in Arsenal’s game against Everton and every time Everton had the ball anywhere near the touchline on his side, he was like joining in the press — his toes are on the touchline. As fourth official, it’s a nightmare, because if you step forward and do anything about it, you’re being pedantic, being petty. He does get away with rather too much. The officials do need to be a bit tighter. And I was one of them who let him do that. I’m not going to deny that. But he was just hard work. Really, really hard work all the time in a way that others tended to be hard work some of the time.”

The Mag Podcast Episode 16: Newcastle United 2008-09 Chaos, Kevin Keegan and Relegation

Published: 13/11/2026 | Duration: 51 mins | Hosts: Jamie Smith, Simon Cahill & David Hutchinson

In Episode 16 of The Mag Pod, we find Jamie, Simon, and Hutch discussing relegation! Special focus is on the 2008-09 season when the combined efforts of Mike Ashley and Dennis Wise forced Kevin Keegan out and a drop to the Championship was the eventual result. So how does the current 2026-27 NUFC situation compare…?

You can play episode 16 on the audio player above or use your favourite podcast platforms including Spotify, Apple Podcasts, Amazon Music, YouTube, and Acast.

Listen to the latest episode of The Mag Pod! Join Jamie, Simon, and Hutch for unfiltered football debate.

Newcastle United’s disastrous 2008-09 relegation season is back under the microscope as Jamie Smith, Simon Cahill and David Hutchinson revisit the chaos of Kevin Keegan’s departure, Mike Ashley’s ownership and Alan Shearer’s desperate rescue mission.

With Newcastle struggling for consistency in the 2026/27 Premier League season, the lads ask whether history offers any lessons for the current squad – and whether today’s concerns really compare with one of the club’s most turbulent campaigns.

The international break provides a welcome breather from Newcastle’s league struggles, and there’s time for a typically entertaining round up of international action, including Dan Burn and Lewis Hall representing England and Yoane Wissa finding the net for DR Congo. Managerial upheaval elsewhere in the Premier League also provides plenty of ammunition, particularly Manchester United’s latest troubles.

Then it’s back to 2008-09, when optimism surrounding Keegan’s return quickly unravelled into protests, questionable transfers and a succession of managerial changes.

Jamie recalls the toxic atmosphere following the exit of Kevin Keegan, the controversial roles of Dennis Wise and Tony Jimenez, and the extraordinary collection of players who somehow ended up relegated.

From Shay Given’s departure and Joe Kinnear’s eventful spell to Alan Shearer’s arrival with just eight matches remaining, the discussion explores where Newcastle’s season went wrong. There’s also time to remember some miserable away trips, controversial refereeing decisions and the players who eventually helped restore pride in the Championship.

Crucially, the lads compare that relegated side with Newcastle’s current squad, examining leadership, creativity, commitment and the importance of stability. Could the same mistakes happen again, or are today’s foundations considerably stronger?

With more historical comparisons planned throughout the international break, this opening instalment combines painful memories, plenty of gallows humour and a surprisingly reassuring perspective on Newcastle United’s present predicament.

#2009. Scott Parker Reunion Could Be Key to West Ham Defensive Deal

No sooner had Scott Parker been appointed as West Ham’s ‘promotion specialist’ manager than stories surfaced linking him with the recruitment of former players.

Reports linking West Ham with C J Egan-Riley are unlikely to disappear anytime soon, with the former Burnley defender continuing to attract attention following his rapid development this season.

Egan-Riley enjoyed a breakthrough campaign previously under Scott Parker, establishing himself as one of the Championship’s standout young defenders and helping Burnley secure promotion back to the Premier League.

A move to the London Stadium would carry several attractions. Not only does Parker know the player well from their time together at Burnley, but Egan-Riley would also qualify as a home-grown player, an increasingly valuable asset for West Ham who are looking to balance squad registration requirements.

Parker has consistently praised the defender in the past, and stated he was a key player for him in the Championship. He was instrumental in the defender’s development, giving him a prominent role in Burnley’s promotion-winning side. His composure on the ball, ability to play across the back line and potential for further improvement make him the type of profile West Ham are expected to target.

Defensive stalwart for Scott Parker’s West Ham?

The central defender chose Marseille ahead of West Ham in 2025, who secured his signature on a free transfer after the expiry of his Burnley contract, meaning any transfer fee received would represent a substantial profit on their investment.

Having been a bit part player at the French club in his first season, following a squad overhaul in the summer he is now a regular starter and the data shows he has maintained a 93% pass completion in Ligue 1. The 23 year old ranks as one of the leagues most accurate passers in his position.

There is also reason to believe Marseille would be willing sellers. The French giants have made no secret of the fact that they will need to generate funds through player departures during the January transfer window due to ongoing financial issues. West Ham have enjoyed a productive relationship with Marseille over the years, with deals for Dimitri Payet, Emerson and Nayef Aguerd demonstrating that negotiations between the two clubs are far from uncommon.

The structure of any potential deal, be it an initial loan or a straight transfer, is yet to emerge. Either way, if the Hammers can persuade the defender to play a part in their quest for promotion they would be adding a young, home-grown centre-back who appears far from reaching his full potential.

I have been a season ticket holder since the late eighties, so experienced the highs and lows of being a West Ham supporter. I previously wrote for OLAS and have contributed to a number of football publications in the past.

#2008. “Cashing in” on Castellanos claim ignores one major stumbling block | West Ham News

Ever since the closing days of the summer transfer window there have been claims that West Ham will be cashing in on Taty Castellanos in the winter: The Argentine has been a huge disappointment in the 15 games of West Ham’s championship season, with just a solitary goal to show for his efforts.

At times he’s resembled more of a moody, disinterested bystander and seems pretty much the most likely player in the eleven to be yellow carded each time he plays.

A solitary goal is plain unacceptable for the frontman who cost £27 million: Claims that he’ll be sold in the winter abound.

Sadly, Everton’s late interest in the summer window, reportedly around £40 million, appears to have evaporated as Taty’s form has waned. Understandably.

Far from happy: One goal in fifteen means Castellanos has been a huge let down in the second tier. Its also means those big money suitors have now evaporated

The newest suggestions from EFL specialist site the72.co.uk suggest Castellanos could be heading back home – however there’s a catch:

“River Plate reportedly view the 28-year-old as a priority target in their striker search, although the finances involved in the deal could prove to be a major hurdle. However, cashing in could give WHUFC the chance to sign a true talisman to aid their promotion bid. “

“Cashing in”? I think not: That’s the elephant in the room here. River Plate have already disclosed that they’ll look at some kind of loan or shared purchase option – as they’re short of funds – which of course will cut no ice with West Ham who will want to replace Taty with a striker more suited to scoring the Championship goals they require.

Merely shipping Taty out on loan without a permanent sale will serve no useful purpose and could actually weaken Scott Parker’s squad. The Hammers have enough loaned – out unwanted stars as it is: Another one added to the list won’t help a rebuild. The only possible route could involve a swap for goal keeper Santiago Beltran – which would still leave the Hammers short of a goal scorer and needing to offload Hermansen or Areola in the winter.

And how often to these player swaps ever come off? Exactly.

#2007. Premier League KMI panel issues emphatic verdict on Alexander Isak penalty decision v Arsenal

The Premier League’s Key Match Incidents (KMI) Panel has concluded that Liverpool should’ve had a penalty awarded for an offence by Jurrien Timber on Alexander Isak in their defeat to Arsenal earlier this month.

Five minutes after Kai Havertz scored the only goal of the game at Anfield, the Swedish striker had his shirt pulled in the box by the Gunners defender, but neither on-field referee Andy Madley nor Stuart Attwell on VAR felt compelled to award a spot kick despite the transgression being clear.

The Reds’ head coach Andoni Iraola went as far as claiming that a penalty would’ve been awarded had our number 9 gone to ground instead of staying on his feet when his jersey was grabbed.

On Wednesday, the Premier League published the findings of several incidents reviewed by the KMI Panel, including the one involving Isak and Timber on 1 November.

Their verdict reads (via premierleague.com): ‘The panel felt that a penalty should have been awarded for a holding action by Timber on Isak, 4:1. One panellist considered the short-lived holding to lack clear impact on the ability of Isak to progress.

‘The majority also felt that VAR should have intervened to recommend an on-field review, 3:2, on the basis that it was a clear and obvious error. Two panellists considered that the subjectivity in assessing impact meant this did not meet the high threshold for VAR intervention.’

The KMI Panel concluded: ‘In this instance the panel deemed that Timber’s challenge on Isak met the threshold for a holding offence and should have resulted in a penalty kick, both on-field and through VAR intervention.’

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

How nice of the KMI Panel to come back and tell us what was so damn obvious at the time of the incident – or at least obvious to anyone not named Andy Madley or Stuart Attwell, or whichever member of the panel felt that the right decision was made on the day.

How that individual concluded that Timber’s actions lacked ‘clear impact on the ability of Isak to progress’ is baffling – the Liverpool striker would surely have gotten on the end of Bradley Barcola’s cross had his shirt not been so blatantly pulled.

The panel’s verdict today won’t come as much consolation to anyone involved with the Reds, who were deprived of a legitimate penalty which – if converted – could’ve significantly altered the course of a match that they lost 1-0.

It’s not much good being told in retrospect that the officials got it wrong; these are clear decisions that professional referees should be capable of getting correct at the time, especially when they have the fallback option of VAR.

We get that many incidents are subjective and that consensus will never be achieved when it comes to refereeing in the Premier League, but there’s simply no excuse for botching calls like the Timber/Isak incident 10 days ago.

#2006. ‘Right now…’ – Liverpool-linked Premier League star makes his plans clear amid transfer rumours

One Premier League player who’s reportedly being targeted by Liverpool has issued a reponse to the transfer speculation surrounding him.

Earlier this week, TEAMtalk claimed that Anfield chiefs are eyeing Bart Verbruggen as a potential long-term successor to Alisson Becker, who’s now 34 and – as it stands – will be out of contract in seven months’ time.

The Brighton goalkeeper was reportedly among a shortlist of candidates being considered by the Reds prior to the summer transfer window, with the Merseysiders eventually agreeing a deal to sign Lucca Brughmans, who’ll join from Genk next summer.

Verbruggen – who’s currently with the Netherlands squad for their concluding UEFA Nations League fixtures – has insisted that despite the rumoured interest from Liverpool, he’s more than happy with the Seagulls, who currently sit second in the Premier League.

The 24-year-old said (via NOS): “Right now we’re doing really well at Brighton, so it would be a real shame to ruin that by living in the future. I really try to stay in the moment, to focus on what is currently going on. I enjoy that, and that is also how I perform best.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Brighton’s magnificent season so far has been underpinned by the excellence of the man between the sticks, who’s kept seven clean sheets in 10 league games and conceded just three times in eight top-flight matches since a 4-3 defeat at Chelsea in August (Transfermarkt).

Figures from Fotmob show that he’s prevented 4.39 xG worth of goals for his team, more than anyone else in the Premier League, and he put in a heroic display in the Seagulls’ recent win at Manchester City as he recorded no fewer than seven saves (Sky Sports).

Those performance levels would indicate that he’d be an ideal successor to Alisson, although there’s been renewed hope in recent days that Liverpool’s number 1 could extend his contract for another year or two, with his agent currently in talks with the club to that effect.

Giorgi Mamardashvili was signed with the intention of succeeding the Brazilian eventually, although the 26-year-old hasn’t always convinced during his time with the Reds so far, and Brughmans will add to the queue once he joins ahead of next season.

Right now there wouldn’t seem to be any urgent need for LFC to move heaven and earth to sign Verbruggen, but if circumstances were to change regarding their current goalkeeping options, it could be worth keeping a hand in should the opportunity arise to move for the Brighton stopper.

#2005. Man United 4-4 Aston Villa PLAYER RATINGS: Who looks like the only ray of light at Old Trafford? Whose display was a mess? And which 3/10 star was absolutely hopeless?

Published: 13:52 EST, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 15:31 EST, 8 November 2026

Manchester United will rot 18th in the Premier League table during the international break even after scrambling an unlikely 4-4 draw against Aston Villa.

Michael Carrick's side fought back from a two-goal deficit, inflicted in just four first-half minutes, and went into the interval level after goals from Bruno Fernandes and Youri Tielemans.

They had to pull off the trick a second time after John McGinn's penalty and Leon Goretzka's back-post tap-in made it 4-2 to Unai Emery's visitors.

But Carrick's side refused to throw in the towel despite how hopeless they were for the majority of this game and his substitutes paid off handsomely.

Joshua Zirkzee made it 4-3 in the 92nd minute, teed up by fellow sub Patrick Dorgu, and Dorgu completed the comeback with a 96th-minute finish of his own to send Old Trafford into raptures.

CEO Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox celebrated in the directors' box, all while Emery stormed off down the tunnel before the final whistle.

Daily Mail Sport's NATHAN SALT was in position at Old Trafford to grade both sets of players...

Patrick Dorgu (right) salvaged the most unlikely of points for Manchester United on Sunday

John McGinn (right) was immense but Villa suffered when he went off as they finished 4-4

A mess of a performance. The Belgian got totally muddled up when he tried to save Alysson's first-minute shot with his knees and it flew between his legs. He could then only parry Alysson's shot straight to Jackson, who made it 2-0. Sold short by his defenders for goals three and four but the United malaise seems to have worn down Lammens, who looked so good last season.

Looked like a rabbit in headlights at the start of the game as the ball ricocheted off him en route to Alysson making it 1-0. Did get an assist for cutting the ball back to Tielemans just before half-time but as an overall performance, Villa feasted on his shortcomings.

Looked like the only United defender capable of defending to a respectable level until even he got sucked into the mistake-fest that United put on at the back. A positive first half, in which he made a strong recovery run to deny Jackson racing through for a third goal, was undone when he inexplicably headed onto his own bar under no pressure to gift Villa a fourth as Leon Goretzka turned in the knockdown.

Made a key last-man challenge but otherwise this was another game where he hasn't been able to organise a defence that is crying out for leadership. Forced off at half-time just days after appearing to tweak his hamstring against Roma.

Absolutely hopeless, just as he was against Roma on Tuesday. Switched off in the first minute and made a weak attempt to block Alysson, who scored. Then, two minutes into the second half, he recklessly fouled Alysson to give away a penalty. Many fans cheered when he was substituted. There has to be a better left back solution than Dalot right now.

Thousands of United fans cheered at the announcement that Diogo Dalot was going off

Scored his first goal for United, and against his former side no less. When United were rolling, Tielemans was at the heart of it all. Faded in the second half when Villa took the lead again and he was unsurprisingly taken off as Carrick's first substitution.

Neat and tidy on the ball but got bested by McGinn for the time the Scottish was on the pitch. One of the few who genuinely does look to play forwards when possible.

His goal drought goes on as we rapidly approach a year since his last one. He's electric when he's bearing down on a full-back and he had to score when played in by Tielemans after escaping the sight of Maatsen. Does so much well but his end product simply must improve or he won't merit starts.

Scored a penalty for the second time in a week but cut a frustrated figure for large spells here as the team collapsed. His corner onto the head of Dorgu was the type of quality you need in crunch moments and that's why he rarely comes off.

Looks like the only ray of light these days as this feckless United side fall to even greater depths. Did well to wrestle himself free of Harwood-Bellis to break and win a penalty after a clueless foul from Boubacar Kamara. Stung the palms of Suzuki soon after.

Matheus Cunha dragged United back into the game and did brilliantly to win an early penalty

Didn't do enough to trouble Villa's backline as he once again found himself deployed down the middle. Only took three shots in this basketball-type game.

Could only scratch his chin in disbelief 60 seconds in when Villa took the lead and he looked down and out when it became 4-2 early in the second half. But he was proactive with his substitutions and they all paid off. He deserves credit for that.

Booked for a reckless - and late - lunge. Interesting he got the nod ahead of Matthijs de Ligt at half-time.

Goal and assist off the bench. Has to be the starter at left back from here on out or United will remain in a washing machine cycle of misery defensively.

Drew a furious response when he ballooned a shot over the bar when United were chasing the game late on.

Electric, again. He's fearless and United have needed that this week when the chips were down.

Joshua Zirkzee (for Bryan Mbeumo, 83) - 7

Clinical when the chance came and it was his goal at 4-3 that gave United the opportunity to stage a dramatic late finish. He gives them a focal point that they are crying out for.

Conceded four times and was livid at the end that VAR didn't punish Lammens backing in to him with the last action of the game. It was a performance that saw Suzuki make some huge saves in the first half. There was one big right hand to deny Amad just before half-time and he was also full stretch to tip Cunha's curling shot away, too, just before. Couldn't see Tielemans' equaliser at 2-2 with Mbeumo in front and will feel aggrieved at the finale.

First Premier League start for Villa since his £30million summer switch and he will have not expected for it to come at right back. Found himself in an unfortunate mismatch against Cunha and the ease at which the Brazilian brushed him off shows why it's unlikely to be a long-term assignment given the quality of wide players in the league.

Was so often given the mocking treatment that has now fallen onto the likes of Dalot and Mazraoui during his time at Manchester United but Lindelof is a better player than many here care to admit. Reads the game well and did well to cut out a run into the box by Patrick Dorgu ten minutes from time but was found wanting on the final set piece that triggered the equaliser.

Victor Lindelof is a better player than a lot of United fans may care to admit

Felt like a quarterback for this Villa side for most of it with how many touches he was able to take under very little pressure. Had a big smile on his face for long spells but that was firmly washed off by the end. Abysmal marking as the game entered stoppage time and both Zirkzee and Dorgu scored.

Was given a torrid time by Amad in the first half and still gives opponents too many opportunities to get at him. Shea Lacey had his way with him when he came on, too. Defensively not good enough.

Spent years getting linked to Manchester United but now here as an opposition player, he made them pay with a goal at the Stretford End to make it 4-2. Tidy player.

Idiotic foul to bring Cunha down to give United a lifeline in a game they weren't in 15 minutes in. Seemed to be caught in two minds whether to push onto Tielemans or Mainoo in the 30-minute spell where United looked like a competent football team. Breathed a sigh of relief when the hosts resorted to type.

A total menace that knew within seconds that he had the beating of Dalot each and every time. Clinical strike in the opening minute to give Villa the lead and his trickery and directness paid off a second time at the start of the second half when he baited Dalot into conceding a penalty. Brilliant outing.

Alysson won a penalty after outwitting Diogo Dalot in the United box early in the second half

Best player on the pitch. He made the right decision time after time and even when pressed on the ball when United started to find a groove, he looked to have unshakeable composure. Cool as you like to score a penalty in front of the Stretford End – not least having missed a penalty against Fulham – and then it was his free-kick that led to the fourth. Still feels underrated.

A fearless dribbler that has the potential to be the jewel of this Villa crown in the years to come. In a league that has long ground a lot of flair players down, his physical dribbling through the lines is a sight to behold. Completed more dribbles than any other player by the time he came off.

Quick as a flash to score from Lammens' spill four minutes in and really should have done better when he was played through one v one, only to see Yoro beat him for pace. Led the line in a way that Manchester United were crying out for.

Has never won at Old Trafford as Villa boss and this is the most regrettable of the lot having led both 2-0 and 4-2 here, only to throw it away in both halves. He stormed off furiously before the final whistle.

#2004. 'It's extremely aggressive' - Stefan Borson drops '£900m' Crystal Palace takeover verdict

Crystal Palace's owners will struggle to find someone to spend £900million on a team at the bottom of the Premier League.

That is according to former Manchester City financial adviser Stefan Borson, who exclusively told Football Insider that now is not the right time for the Eagles to change owners.

Palace are in the midst of an enormous storm, having just sacked Pierre Sage after 16 games, leaving them 20th in the league standings.

After drawing 1-1 with Hoffenheim, the 2024-25 FA Cup winners are also sitting 21st in the Europa League table after four matches.

There is now a very big fear that the Eagles could be relegated this season, and it remains to be seen who could replace Sage in the dugout during this international break.

As well as failures on the pitch, the owners have also been unable to find any potential buyers for the club, having valued Palace at £900m.

Speaking exclusively to Football Insider, Borson has sent some home truths to Selhurst Park after it was revealed that as many as eight Premier League clubs are up for sale, officially or unofficially.

"Some of the clubs that are on the list are not going to get deals. I think, you take Crystal Palace, for example..." he said.

"I don't think anybody's going to buy Crystal Palace for £900m at the bottom of the table. First of all, the price was always extremely aggressive.

"And secondly, I just don't think now is the right time for them. So I think it's more about who isn't going to get sold on that list."

It has been reported that the Eagles' owners are exploring a full sale, but it remains to be seen who else is on that newly emerging, and hidden, list.

It's impossible to put an exact figure on that question, in all fairness, but it does seem like Palace's owners are asking for above the market value.

To put it into perspective, Everton have a new stadium and are sixth in the Premier League, and The Friedkin Group (TFG) are asking for £1billion.

Borson, therefore, believes that Palace's owners should be asking in the region of £750m to £800m, and might attract more buyers this season.

Palace won trophies in back-to-back seasons, the FA Cup in 2024-25 and the Europa Conference League in 2025-26. Now, relegation is on the cards.

Celtic are not considering the sale of Mika Baur as a possibility in the January transfer window, sources have told Football Insider.

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 15:38 EST, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 15:38 EST, 8 November 2026

Martin O’Neill faces an anxious wait to discover the full extent of Mika Baur’s ankle injury after the midfielder hobbled off in distress late in their win against Kilmarnock.

Celtic re-established their four-point lead at the top of the Premiership with a 1-0 victory over the Premiership’s bottom club courtesy of Liam Scales’ first-half strike.

But the outcome was achieved amid concern for the German who failed to recover from a late tackle by visiting midfielder Aaron Tshibola.

Baur, who’s been outstanding since joining from Paderborn in the summer, is due to join up with Germany’s Under-21s for their games with Belgium and Croatia but will now wait to discover the full extent of the injury.

‘He’s in the treatment room,’ said O’Neill. ‘His ankle is really sore and we don’t know the damage. We’ll wait until tomorrow to get a scan.

‘Gosh, I’d hope he won’t be out terribly long, but I don’t know at the moment.

Celtic midfielder Mika Baur goes down clutching his ankle after a late tackle by Aaron Tshibola

Celtic manager Martin O'Neill hopes that the injury will not sideline Baur for a lengthy period

Kilmarnock boss Neil McCann believes his side are capable of climbing the Premiership table

‘He’s been great for us considering he’s not the tallest. He’d be about ten stone, maybe not even that, but his workrate is incredible. His overall reading of the game is really good and he’s not frightened.’

O’Neill felt his players made life difficult for themselves with Benjamin Nygren’s penalty miss in the second half typifying their lack of composure in front of goal.

‘Pleased to win,’ he added. ‘It was a tough afternoon. We could never could put the game to bed and Kilmarnock were always in the game.

‘They played exceptionally well at times. Even (aside from) missing the penalty, it was really uncomfortable. But we saw it through. And after the effort on Thursday (against Besiktas), I probably wasn’t surprised that we didn’t have the same driving energy through the game. It was important to win.’

Kasper Hogh thought he’d put an end to his 16-game run without a goal when he netted in the first half only for VAR to pick up on an earlier foul by Baur on Greg Kiltie.

‘I thought Kasper was off the mark for about 35 seconds,’ O’Neill reflected. ‘I think he would maybe have scored the next chance if the first had counted, but he worked really hard for us.’

Despite failing to score, Hogh’s all-round contribution was recognised by a warm reception from supporters when he was substituted.

‘That’s really encouraging,’ said O’Neill. ‘If you have the crowd behind you then you feel that if you’re working hard they’ll forgive other things.

‘It won’t last forever. Strikers live and die by their goals but we all believe in him in the dressing room which is very encouraging.

‘In front of goal, it’s difficult. But he worked exceptionally hard, as he did on Thursday. I think things will come. His hold-up play is much better now.’

O’Neill was asked why Haissem Hassan didn’t figure at all in the match-day squad.

‘We’re trying to do as much manoeuvring as possible,’ he explained. ‘If there is proper competition for places it can only make it better.’

Jota made his first Celtic start since April of last year, lasting 45 minutes. O’Neill said: ‘I didn’t expect him to last. I thought he might get 60 minutes but he was tiring before half-time.

‘I said I didn’t expect him to go the whole way. Yang (Hyun-jun) was ready to go. He’s been brilliant for us this season.’

Despite failing to take any points from the match, Kilmarnock manager Neil McCann felt his side’s performance was brimming with positives.

‘The boys were brilliant,’ he said. ‘It’s not an easy place to come, especially after Celtic’s good result against Besiktas and them having their tails up and being confident.

‘We created chances, we were disciplined and brave on the ball in a difficult environment. The boys are really disappointed we didn’t take anything.

‘I know there was a penalty saved which was a really harsh decision when it’s given, but outside that I thought we were comfortable.

‘We came away with nothing, but when you reflect there are so many good things to take and get a head of steam up.

‘If we catch some breaks and be more ruthless, we’ll start climbing the table. There’s not a lot between everyone and that’s why I have optimism.’

In quotes published by the print edition of Blikk (via Sport Witness), ex-Hungary goalkeeper Janos Csank blasted Iraola for not substituting Szoboszlai at half-time in the win over Palace.

The 80-year-old raged: “I was really annoyed. Szoboszlai went down on the pitch in the first half, and at half-time I was certain he wouldn’t come back on for the second half. Then I saw him standing there on the pitch, with black tape on his leg, his knee.

“Then the manager starts sobbing that he is injured. He should have been substituted straight away; they were leading 1-0. Half-time comes and then he sends him back on injured with his knee bandaged?! I’m losing my mind! I just don’t get it.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

As head coach of Liverpool, the club to whom Szoboszlai is contracted, Iraola is well within his rights to utilise the player as he sees fit, and any decision to send him back out for the second half would surely have been taken in consultation with the medical staff.

We admit that, if that had happened on international duty, we’d be pleading for Marco Rossi to exercise caution and substitute the 26-year-old immediately. Every stakeholder will inevitably shout the loudest in favour of their best interests.

In a similar vein, Reds supporters will hope that the midfielder isn’t deemed fit enough to play for his country in the coming week and instead recover for the Manchester United game the following Sunday, whereas he’ll be striving to prove his fitness in time to face Georgia on Saturday.

Szoboszlai has almost always been available during his three-and-a-bit years as a Liverpool player, although he’s had an injury-hit few weeks of late, having only recently overcome a thigh problem which resurfaced during the win at Brentford last month.

Everyone of a Reds persuasion will face a nervous wait over the next week or so to see whether Iraola will have any fresh injury worries once our season resumes in 10 days’ time. Fingers crossed that everyone on international duty gets back to Merseyside unscathed.

#1987. “It’s a special place” – Liverpool confirm Anfield return for James Milner

Liverpool FC have confirmed on Thursday that James Milner will return to Anfield in 2027.

Signed on a free transfer from Manchester City in 2015, the former Reds midfielder spent eight years on Merseyside and became vice-captain under Jurgen Klopp, winning the Premier League and Champions League among other trophies in his time with the club.

The 40-year-old closed out his playing career at Brighton, announcing his retirement this summer after setting the record for the most Premier League seasons appeared in (24 consecutively from 2002/03 to 2025/26).

As announced via liverpoolfc.com on Thursday lunchtime, Milner is the first player to be confirmed for the next Liverpool Legends match, which takes place against Inter Milan at Anfield on Saturday 27 March 2027, with proceeds going towards the LFC Foundation.

The Reds’ former vice-captain said of his participation in the fixture: “I’m thrilled to have the chance to pull on the red shirt again and step back out at Anfield. It’s a special place, and playing there in front of the supporters is a feeling like no other.

“What makes the legends match so special is that it’s about more than football. It’s a chance to give something back to the fans while supporting the work of the LFC Foundation. I’m delighted to be the first to sign up and can’t wait to be part of it.”

#1985. Scotland are failing to dispel emperor’s new clothes concerns after laboured victory

The Scottish Football Association’s ticket promotion drive for this match emphasised that games are always better under the lights. They might need to re-think that one.

This was another endurance test that at least had a satisfactory outcome, courtesy of John McGinn’s double. In between times a goal for North Macedonia - their first in nine games - probably triggered a national holiday back home and made things look very difficult indeed for Sebastien Pocognoli.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Scotland held onto their lead, given to them after McGinn drove into the box following strong centre-forward play from Che Adams, for the best part of three minutes.

A penalty, awarded after a VAR check a good couple of minutes after goalkeeper Stole Dimitrievski's trip on Ben Gannon-Doak occurred, saved Scotland’s blushes with 16 minutes left and kept their Nations League hopes just about alive.

McGinn did the necessary from the spot although Oli McBurnie, who had replaced Adams six minutes earlier, might have appreciated being given the ball in his seemingly eternal quest for an international goal. It was perhaps too important a kick to take any chances. A manager’s future prospects might have rested on it.

It was a case of third time lucky for Pocognoli as he secured his first Hampden win on what had not seemed like a particularly auspicious date. For the first time since the notorious 0-0 draw against Uruguay that torpedoed their 1986 World Cup, Scotland were in action on a Friday the 13th. What could possibly go wrong? A lot, it seemed at times.

If anything underlined that these are very different times for Scotland it was the sight of Scott McTominay, almost a year to the day since that overhead kick against Denmark, launching himself into the air again in an effort to meet Gilmour’s cross. Although he connected well, the direction was lacking. The ball went high over the bar.

There was no goal from the halfway line this time either. Instead, we were treated to one of the worst misses ever seen at Hampden when Gilmour skied the ball from seven yards seconds after the interval.

The Hampden crowd was getting testy. Boos had greeted the half-time whistle, with the score still goalless and the hosts perhaps lucky not to have conceded.

McGinn’s opener ten minutes after half-time seemed like just the medicine. However, underlining how this was never straightforward, Macedonia equalised almost immediately. They had to score a goal sometime but it was not a good look for Scotland or McTominay, who was beaten in the air at the front post by Elmin Rastodar following a corner.

A clumsy challenge at the other end by Dimitrievski on Gannon-Doak, whose poor touch had already looked to have taken the chance away from him, gave Scotland the gratifying chance to equalise from the spot 17 minutes later.

The hosts had endured an uncertain start that was a decent indicator of what lay ahead. What seemed like teething problems might have been attributed to a defence playing together for the first time. Ryan Porteous was brought back into the starting line-up, his first start since the opening match of Euro 2024 when he was sent off.

Luke Graham, meanwhile, earned his second cap - a first start for Scotland - and was planted right in the middle of the three-man backline. After surviving a few shaky moments initially, the Stoke City defender acquitted himself superbly well.

North Macedonia’s dismal run, which included not having scored in this Nations League campaign so far, perhaps convinced Pocognoli he could make such alterations though injury had restricted his options. Poertoeus, though, hadn’t even been named in the original squad.

Defence wasn’t expected to be an issue. It was a Friday night after a long week at work. Fans wanted to be entertained, they wanted to see some tangible evidence of a new Scotland they have been promised. Pocognoli might wear a suit very well but he’s not proved himself to be his predecessor’s equal at obtaining results, although this was more like it. The fear is that this supposedly more free-flowing Scotland has made them blunter. The phrase the emperor’s new clothes could not be banished from the mind.

Not even McTominay could ignite things. He seemed ready to burst the net just a few minutes later after Lewis Ferguson’s header found the Napoli midfielder with his back to goal in the box. When he turned, it looked like there would be only one outcome. However, Dimitrievski made a tremendous save low to his left.

Yes, this was another occasion where the North Macedonian goalkeeper excelled himself, just as he did in Skopje at the start of last month.

Another save, when he plucked a deflected Adams header out from beneath his crossbar, was even better. There were mitigating factors for Scotland failing to make the breakthrough in the opening half.

It might have been worse for the home team. A cute lay-off from Darko Churlinov set up skipper Enis Bardhi, who lashed a left-footed shot into the side-netting. Most of the Hampden crowd feared the ball had gone in. The smattering of North Macedonia fans were beside themselves.

Sadly for them, happily for the vast majority, the rippling effect was due to the ball hitting the wrong side of the net. It might have been marginally offside in any case. Jeers greeted the blowing of the half-time whistle moments later, nonetheless.

Would Scotland come out with a renewed sense of purpose? It seemed so. Adams pounced on a short pass back and cut the ball back while Dimitrievski dithered.

Billy Gilmour is no one’s idea of a prolific goalscorer but even he couldn’t miss from seven yards, goal gaping. He did. Quite incredibly, the ball comfortably cleared the bar. People were referencing Chris Iwelumo, meaning it was one of the worst misses of all time. It was at the right end, certainly. McGinn showed him how to do it, moving level with Hughie Gallacher in third place on 24 goals in the all-time list of goalscorers and ensuring Andy Robertson’s record-equalling 102nd cap would also be the victorious one the skipper deserved.

#1982. Sebastien Pocognoli predicts another Scotland record will be broken and identifies ‘something we need to fix’

Sebastien Pocognoli believes it is only a matter of time until John McGinn becomes Scotland’s all-time top goalscorer.

The Scotland manager saw McGinn score a match-winning double to help Scotland secure a scratchy and often uninspired win over North Macedonia. It handed Pocognoli his first Hampden victory at the third attempt and brought some relief for the Belgian.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

It hadn’t looked good when North Macedonia equalised almost immediately after McGinn had put Scotland ahead after 54 minutes. The header from Elmin Rastoder was the visitors' first goal in nine games.

A penalty from McGinn following a VAR check with 16 minutes left, after goalkeeper Stole Dimitrievski clumsily tripped Ben Gannon-Doak, secured the three points for Scotland and kept their hopes of finishing second in their Nations League group alive. Slovenia drew 0-0 with group winners Switzerland.

Pocognoli’s side must win against Switzerland in St Gallen on Monday and hope Macedonia take something from their clash at home against the Slovenians.

With McGinn in the side, anything is possible against Switzerland. Pocognoli hailed the Aston Villa’s contribution and feels he will shortly overtake Kenny Dalglish and Denis Law in the rankings. Both legends scored 30 goals for Scotland and McGinn, who now sits third with Hughie Gallacher on 24 goals, is now just seven goals from overtaking the pair at the top. He has already scored three goals under Pocognoli, having struck a penalty in the 2-0 win against North Macedonia in Skopje last month.

“I'm more focused on the collective challenge and goals,” said Pocognoli. “And I believe if we can build something nice around the collective, then John will one day break the record. He has had a lot of chances through these five games together already. It's important but the individual record I always bring in the collective package. And I hope for him that he can reach it.”

Pocognoli, if not satisfied with all aspects of Scotland’s play, was happy to end the week “with a good feeling” and before travelling to face Switzerland.

He added: “It was not always perfect, but I know that what we worked in two days (this week) happened many times today on the pitch. That's for me very important. On top of that, we created a lot of chances that we really have to score and maybe have a better feeling after the game. But on the whole, I think we were quite aggressive.”

Billy Gilmour missed an open goal shortly after half-time while Dimitrievski pulled off a number of good saves.

“Off the ball, I think we were quite aggressive,” said Pocognoli, who handed a full debut to Stoke City’s Luke Graham in the centre of a three-man defence. “We recover a number of balls that we managed well in some moments of transition.

"We created a big chance for Billy [Gilmour] from this also. So that's a new approach of the game. I think we started the game not that intensely because we didn't manage the ball well. And then for sure you start the game with the feeling that we don't control the ball. After 10 minutes we started to reach Lewis [Ferguson] and Billy [Gilmour] through the lines. And then the game became what we expected.

‘We created chances, we isolated Ben [Gannon-Doak] in the one v one, and we had a lot of pressure. After the first goal I think we need to learn not to drop the intensity. Because after the first goal for 5 minutes I really feel like we dropped the intensity and the focus.

“And we had the same feeling after the second one. So, it's something that we need to fix.”

He agreed Scotland need to be more clinical. “Yes, probably,” he said, while perhaps recalling the missed chances against Slovenia in his first match in charge and which now seem so significant.

‘But I prefer to talk about creating a lot of chances,” he added. “And probably we should keep a clean sheet. So that's really the critical aspect and the demanding aspect. But it's part of the challenge and we are early in the challenge to try to fix this for the future.”

#1980. Michael Carrick clashes with Sky Sports reporter in spiky interview over his future: Man United boss expects to continue despite club being in relegation zone after 4-4 draw with Villa

By CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER and LUKE AUGUSTUS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 15:17 EST, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 16:08 EST, 8 November 2026

Michael Carrick insists he won't quit as Manchester United boss despite having to see his team spend the international break in the relegation zone.

United staged another incredible fightback to snatch a 4-4 draw with Aston Villa at Old Trafford after trailing by two goals heading into injury-time.

But it wasn't enough to spare the club from the humiliation of being in the bottom three for the next two weeks – the longest United have spent there since 1986.

The manner of the performance and result will only heap further pressure on Carrick and when the future of his own position was put to him by Sky Sports reporter Patrick Davison, the United boss took exception to the question in a spiky interview.

'What do you expect to happen over the next few weeks? You've been asked time and again about your future? I know you have said that you walking away was the best for the club, you'd probably do it,' Davison asked Carrick.

'It's not going to happen, no,' Carrick replied.

"That's not going to happen" 🗣️Michael Carrick responds to the notion that he could resign as Manchester United head coach 🔴 pic.twitter.com/q1fBKSXL7l

Michael Carrick was involved in a spiky interview with Sky Sports about his Man United future

Patrick Dorgu (centre) scored a late equaliser as troubled Man United drew 4-4 vs Aston Villa

Despite Sunday's draw, Carrick's position as United head coach looks increasingly doubtful

With United chiefs Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox in the stands, Davison pushed further asking: 'What do you expect to happen? Clearly there's going to be conversation?'

This prompted Carrick to quizzically state: 'Is there?' as the pair engaged in a back-and-forth on the subject.

Eventually Carrick replied: 'You know the situation, we haven't won enough games. But I expect to move forward with things we've been working on, showing a lot of the good from today tighten up a few mistakes and win some football matches.'

United's start of one win in 10 games is still their worst since Alex Ferguson replaced Ron Atkinson 40 years ago this week. They conceded twice at the start of each half against Villa, and have now let in 30 goals in all competitions – the joint highest in Europe's top five leagues.

'We're making it hard for ourselves. Mistakes that the boys know shouldn't happen,' added Carrick. 'Two goals again put us on the back foot. We beat ourselves a little bit with the goals that we're giving away in tight clusters. It's hard enough anyway, but we're making it a lot more difficult than it should be.

'I thought we were the better team. We never gave up and never stopped believing. I'm disappointed that we still haven't won the game, to be truthful.'

The United fans kept behind Carrick and his team while once again targeting the club's owners, chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox.

However, there were loud cheers when Diogo Dalot was replaced in the 66th minute. It was reminiscent of the treatment of Joshua Zirkzee by the home supporters when he was substituted against Newcastle in December 2024, and the Dutchman made a point of giving Dalot a reassuring hug in the dugout.

'We've got to be careful with that,' said Carrick. 'I understand the frustration and the disappointment of the supporters, so I get it. We're all frustrated, we're all disappointed, and the players are as much as anyone, I guarantee you that.

'Diogo gives absolutely everything. He's played in different positions, he's played left-back, he's played really well at times.

'He gave a penalty away today, he knows that. Maybe he can do a little bit better. He's made a mistake, but he cares an awful lot and he's giving everything.'

Dalot's replacement Patrick Dorgu led the fightback, five days after United had recovered from two goals down to beat Roma 3-2, as he crossed for Zirkzee to pull a goal back and then headed the equaliser in the 96th minute.

'I don't feel happy,' said Dorgu. 'We are in a bad situation and we need to fight together to get out of it. A draw is better than a loss, but everyone needs to look at themselves and ask if they are doing enough. We need to fight for the manager, for the club and get out of this together.

'Of course, it hurts (to be in relegation zone). There are a lot of games and we need everyone to come back sharp from international break and start getting wins.'

Teammate Matheus Cunha added: 'We are so disappointed. Before anything else we need to look inside to us – the players, the staff. It's a huge club and to feel something like this (being in the relegation zone) is not normal.'

It's not the first time Carrick has engaged in an interesting post-match interview this season. In August, he snapped at a reporter's 'ridiculous' opening question after Manchester United's shock defeat at Hull City on the opening day of the season.

Carrick was affronted when asked if his players had lost against the newly promoted club due to a lack of 'passion'.

United's Premier League season got off to a nightmare start as goals from Semi Ajayi and Nobel Mendy - both stemming from set-pieces - put them to the sword in Yorkshire.

Carrick was interviewed afterwards by Viaplay broadcaster Jan Age Fjortoft, the Norwegian who played for Swindon, Middlesbrough, Sheffield United and Barnsley in the 1990s.

“Come on, that’s ridiculous.”Michael Carrick wasn’t happy when asked if there was a lack of passion from #mufc in their first half vs Hull.via @ViaplayFotball pic.twitter.com/zyca5r5iSr

In August, Carrick said it was 'ridiculous' to suggest United lacked passion after losing to Hull

He was vexed by the question posed by Viaplay reporter and former play Jan Age Fjortoft

'Would you accept that there was a lack of passion in the first half?' asked Fjortoft.

'Oh come on, that's ridiculous,' Carrick hit back.

'That's not how you would assess it?' asked Fjortoft.

Carrick replied: 'Come on, you played football, you understand, that's a ridiculous thing to say. Just because you got beat doesn't mean you don't care about it.'

Fjortoft said: 'I'm not saying that you didn't care about it. If you look at it, they came with passion, that's what I mean. I understand that you care about it, but would you accept that they took you on that front, so to say?'

'No, no. Their two goals came from set plays. Other than that, we had opportunities,' Carrick said. 'That was where the game was. I don't think it was passion or anything to do with that. I think it was just their moment that made the difference in the game.'

Fjortoft said: 'Is it these duels? Is that what you mean? That these two duels were the goals? Because they had chances. There were consequences there from the game that you could see that they would get at you.'

'It's a game of football, it's a Premier League game,' Carrick replied.

'It's their first game at home, and we've seen it many times before. You know, I said it before the game because it was always going to be a tough game.

'And set-plays, yeah, that's it. We've been decent over a period of time at dealing with them, and today we didn't.

'We can look into that, we can dissect it. We certainly won't get carried away with the positives or the negatives. We never do. So I think we can stay calm and understand what we need to get better at.'

After the international break though United face the ultimate litmus test when they travel to bitter rivals Liverpool at Anfield in the Premier League on November 22.

#1975. Sheffield Wednesday v Plymouth Argyle: Dave Challinor wants more than silver lining from first real Owls test

When the 51-year-old agreed to become Sheffield Wednesday’s next manager, it was not for nights like last Sunday, when his team went out of the FA Cup at Oldham Athletic in the first round's graveyard slot, suited only to the television companies.

And his maiden game at Hillsborough was a first-team game in little more than name only.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

He watched a team containing at best two or three players who will feature on Saturday lose 4-0 to another League Two side, Accrington Stanley, knowing they were through to the last 32 of the Football League Trophy regardless. Only 5,472 die-hards were there.

Plymouth Argyle, genuine promotion rivals under Bradfordian Tom Cleverley are in town.

At the best of times, when Hi Ho Silver Lining belts out, clapped and sung along to by a crowd of 30,000, it makes the hairs on the back of your neck stand up. When you are experiencing it for the first time as Sheffield Wednesday manager, it must be doubly special.

"I can't wait," says Challinor, whose managerial apprenticeship began in the footballing backwaters of Colwyn Bay and Fylde before progressing to the more established Hartlepool United and Stockport County.

"Even the anthem at the start of the game with, I'm not sure how many were in there on Wednesday but it's still a big noise from behind you (the main stand was the only home section open) with a less than half-empty stadium.

"To be able to experience and witness that at the weekend is something I'm looking forward to.

"It's special, I think, when you go to many football grounds and there's the songs that are sung at the start of games, it provides a special atmosphere.

"For me to be stood there in the home dugout and it be sung by our supporters to our team, makes it that more special.

"It’s something I'm really looking forward to. "

With that comes responsibilities, as Challinor is aware.

Defeat last Sunday was mildly embarrassing, but quickly got over. The midweek loss will barely have registered with some, not at all with others.

But even though history is against him – the Owls have always needed at least a second season to get out of the third tier – Challinor is expected to win promotion from League One this season, so sentiment will quickly turn to anger if his side do not play a lot better than in his first two matches.

"What happens on the pitch after the singing of Hi Ho Silver Lining is going to be imperative," stresses the new manager.

"Straight away, the focus will be on what the game looks like and hopefully putting in a performance that can build momentum and get a run going.

"The challenge that (managing a "big club") brings is something that, for me, personally, was the next thing I need to do for myself.

"The opportunity to come here and be part of something and build something, being part of it, the fanbase, is a great opportunity and one I'm desperate to take."

Even at 3pm on Saturday, it will not be the full-strength Dave Challinor Sheffield Wednesday, with the injury list running into double figures in midweek. Max Lowe, ruled out for four to six weeks with another hamstring problem, is the latest addition.

"We're hoping that Lummers (goalkeeper Joe Lumley) will be back with us really soon, possibly at the weekend," said Challinor that night. "He's done some training with us this week and has ticked off most things.

"He'd be really important because of the experience and the level that he's played at.

"But if that's not the case, Connal (Trueman)'s an able deputy and I'm sure will do a really good job for us.

"Coops (Liam Cooper) trained this week, Billy (Mitchell) and Louie Barry similarly. Th weekend probably comes too soon for Ali (Al-Hamadi). The others, we've got a decision to make.

"It's a massively important game and we want them back. We're just going to make sure we get them back and we keep them back. It can't be a cycle of one comes back, one goes out, one comes back because we never get any stronger."

There could be a change from the back three of the first two matches to accommodate players.

"Potentially," says Challinor. "We'll look at all things in terms of how systems work, how you build and what you do in possession is different to what you do out of possession.

"We need to deal with the threats we're going to be posed. We know what Plymouth will come with.

"They'll be direct, they're aggressive at the top end of the pitch. They want to run behind, they'll put crosses in the box.

"We're going to have to stop crosses. We're going to have to defend our box, but we need to also influence them by getting our players in the right areas of the pitch in order to cause them problems.

"So there'll be a little bit of to-ing and fro-ing, but we'll do whatever we feel gives us the best chance of winning the game."

#1972. Steven Gerrard explains his theory on why Alexis Mac Allister has been so resurgent this season

Steven Gerrard has offered a theory as to why Alexis Mac Allister has looked so resurgent this season compared to last.

The midfielder was one of the Reds’ most disappinting players of a dreadful 2025/26 campaign, especially having been such a key component in the preceding Premier League title triumph, but he’s been playing near to his best since Andoni Iraola took charge in the summer.

Speaking on The Overlap Daily (via Liverpool Echo), our former captain claimed that the 27-year-old subconsciously let his performance levels drop last season as he was privately consumed by trying to retain the World Cup with Argentina.

Gerrard said of Mac Allister: “I’ve loved him this season. I think last year, like a lot of the Argentinian players, they had a bit of a distraction with the World Cup coming up.

“It’s the way they are. The World Cup takes over everything in their lives, and I lived that with Emiliano Martínez when I was at Aston Villa. I just think it becomes a priority.

“I think it becomes a bit of a distraction. It becomes the most important thing in their lives, to be ready and not injured and make sure that the national team is the priority.

“I think with a lot of the Argentina players, I’m sure a lot of managers, if they watch this, will say: ‘Yeah, I’ve experienced that.’”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

It’s an interesting theory that Gerrard has put forward to explain why Mac Allister’s performances from last season to this have been so chalk and cheese.

Many footballers consider the World Cup as the pinnacle of their careers, and the Liverpool midfielder represents a nation where the sport is nothing short of an obsession.

Only the 27-year-old could truthfully answer whether or not he let his levels dip in 2025/26 because he was prioritising the global tournament in North America, but from a Reds perspective we’d hope that isn’t the case.

As a player employed by LFC, Mac Allister has a duty to give full commitment to representing the club. As disappointing as his performances were last season, though, we wouldn’t go as far as accusing him of not giving less than 100%, which’d be a serious indictment of an elite footballer.

Thankfully, the Argentine has looked much more like his usual self since August, to the point where Troy Deeney suggested that he would even inspire Liverpool to nudge their way into the Premier League title race if he maintains or improves further upon his current standards.

The 27-year-old has been vocal about his contract situation at Anfield, but if he keeps playing the way that he has been, securing a new deal for him should become a matter of priority for sporting director Richard Hughes.

#1964. Astonishing moment manager HEADBUTTS opposition player and is sent off, sparking mass brawl as FA Cup first round clash descends into chaos

By JAMES DUTTON, DEPUTY SPORTS NEWS EDITOR and WILL GOVE

Published: 16:39 EST, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 16:41 EST, 8 November 2026

Oldham boss Micky Mellon was sent off for headbutting Sheffield Wednesday midfielder Callum Slattery as their FA Cup first round clash descended into a mass brawl at Boundary Park.

League Two Oldham pulled off a shock over their League One opponents, but the result was overshadowed by the altercation which occurred six minutes from the end of normal time.

The former Blackpool and Burnley midfielder appeared to grab Slattery by the back of the neck and pulled him closer to his face, before pushing his head into the rival player’s face and knocking him over.

The touchline soon descended into chaos with players and staff from both teams grappling with each other in a farcical melee.

Eventually the two warring sides were separated giving referee Martin Woods the opportunity to approach Mellon and present him with a thoroughly deserved red card.

Oldham, now with their manager in the stands, played on and incredibly nicked a 110th minute winner through Will Sutton.

Oldham Athletic manager Micky Mellon is shown a red card for moving his head towards Wednesday's Callum Slattery 🟥📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB pic.twitter.com/5QMxgLt0dO

Oldham manager Micky Mellon was sent off for an astonishing headbutt on Sheffield Wednesday midfielder Callum Slattery

The scene soon descended into chaos as both players and staff from both sides entered the melee

Eventually Mellon was shown a red card and will serve a three match touchline ban

Wednesday piled on the pressure in the final minutes desperately trying to find an equaliser but to no avail as Oldham held on and advanced into the next round.

Mellon, however, will now have to serve a three-match touchline ban meaning he will miss his side's next appearance in this year's FA Cup.

Calum Kavanagh had put Oldham ahead in the 66th minute with a fierce drive after Mike Fondop headed on Noah Chilvers’ right-wing cross – his sixth goal of the season.

Wednesday equalised ten minutes later through former Oldham forward Davis Keillor-Dunn.

Elsewhere in the FA Cup on Sunday, seventh-tier Wimborne Town stunned League Two Crawley 2-0 to reach the second round for the first time in their history.

The Dorset part-timers of the Southern League Premier Division South took the lead through Yang Seung-woo’s stunning strike after nine minutes, with Cameron Munn deflecting in Jackson King’s shot 11 minutes from time to seal the upset.

Stockport survived a scare to beat Cray Wanderers of the Isthmian League Premier Division 3-2.

The League One high-flyers were facing a shock exit when they fell two goals behind in the first half, a situation not helped by a red card for goalkeeper Luca Ashby-Hammond for a foul outside the box.

From the free-kick, defender Alex Hernandez found the top corner to make it 2-0, but Stockport staged a late fightback, Kyle Wootton and, in added time, Mikael Mandron scoring to take the tie to extra time before Lewis Fiorini’s penalty won it.

Eighth-tier Stafford Rangers also led EFL opposition 2-0 before bowing out, Grimsby finding themselves facing an embarrassing exit against a team four divisions lower before hitting back to make it 3-3 after extra time, eventually going through on penalties.
