#1963. I watched Scotland limp to victory vs North Macedonia and noted astonishing moment and rising star

Sebastian Pocognoli celebrated his first victory at Hampden as Scotland limped past North Macedonia 2-1 in uninspiring fashion last night.

John McGinn’s second half brace proved decisive to secure three valuable Nations League points and keep Scotland's promotion play-off hopes alive ahead of Monday's trip to Switzerland.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

The Aston Villa midfielder opened the scoring after the break, only for Elmin Rastoder to equalise almost immediately. McGinn then kept his cool from the penalty spot after 73 minutes following a VAR review to restore Scotland's lead and seal a much-needed victory.

Lewis Anderson watched the action unfold in Mount Florida for The Scotsman and picks out his five main takeaways from the game.

This was far from a classic and a bit of a grind, but securing a first win at Hampden Park was an important milestone for Pocognoli as he continues to find his feet in the Scotland hotseat. Having endured a mixed start to his tenure, the Belgian will have been acutely aware of the importance of delivering a positive result in front of an expectant home support against winless opponents ranked 71st in the world, particularly with Scotland's Nations League promotion play-off ambitions hanging in the balance.

After losing his first two home fixtures in charge, the pressure was on the Belgian to deliver. While the performance was far from convincing, with Scotland squandering several opportunities before allowing a North Macedonia side who had failed to score in their previous eight matches to draw level, McGinn's spot-kick ultimately spared their blushes.

There was little comfort in the manner of the victory, but the three points were invaluable. More importantly, Pocognoli can now look to build on his first Hampden success as Scotland prepare for their decisive trip to St. Gallen, knowing that their hopes of reaching the promotion play-offs remain firmly alive.

The ever-reliable McGinn further cemented his place in Scotland's footballing history with his double, taking his international tally to 24 goals and drawing level with Hughie Gallacher in joint-third place on the country's all-time scoring charts list.

He continues to combine his trademark energy and leadership with an impressive knack for finding the net, and is now firmly in pursuit of the players above him. Only Denis Law and Kenny Dalglish remain out in front with 30 goals apiece, leaving McGinn within touching distance of some of the most illustrious names ever to wear the dark blue jersey.

At 32 and with plenty of international football potentially still to come, the prospect of climbing further up the rankings and surpassing that record is an increasingly realistic one.

Luke Graham enjoyed a hugely encouraging first start in the heart of defence, making a positive impression despite having only two international appearances to his name. This was an ideal opportunity for the Stoke City defender to show that he belongs at international level and can become a regular fixture in Pocognoli's plans.

He looked assured in a back three, showing good positional awareness and a willingness to put his body on the line when North Macedonia threatened. The 22-year-old produced an well-timed sliding challenge early in the second half to snuff out a dangerous attack and also came close to adding a goal at the other end, rising highest to meet a Lewis Ferguson corner but glancing his header narrowly wide. His aerial presence offered an additional threat.

Having made the step up from his brief cameo appearance in last month's victory in Skopje, the former Dundee man has given Pocognoli plenty to consider as he looks to establish himself in the senior set-up.

Scotland remain far from the finished article, but Graham’s performance was an encouraging step in the right direction for a player only at the beginning of his international journey.

Less than a minute into the second half, Napoli’s Billy Gilmour blazed over with the goal gaping from eight yards out from a Che Adams cut-back, summing up Scotland's lack of clinical edge in the final third and creating an instant sense of dread inside the national stadium.

For the Tartan Army, watching that golden, unmissable chance go begging at the same end of Hampden instantly triggered flashbacks to October 11, 2008, drawing comparisons to Chris Iwelumo’s infamous blunder from three yards out in a crucial 2010 World Cup qualifier against Norway.

Both glaring misses occurred in high-stakes fixtures where Scotland were struggling to break down stubborn opposition. Just as Iwelumo's error piled immense pressure on manager George Burley, Gilmour's miss threatened to derail Pocognoli's bid for a desperately needed first home win.

While Iwelumo's miss resulted in a costly 0-0 draw that effectively ruined Scotland's qualification campaign and haunted the striker for years, Gilmour was spared lasting infamy by McGinn, turning his horror moment into a lucky escape.

It was a landmark evening for captain Andy Robertson, who earned his 102nd Scotland cap to draw level with the great Kenny Dalglish as the country's most-capped player.

The Tottenham left-back, who has led his country with distinction for several years, now has the opportunity to move clear of Dalglish's long-standing record when Scotland travel to Switzerland on Monday.

It is a terrific achievement for a player who has become such an influential figure in the national side, both on and off the pitch. Having carried the captain's armband through some of Scotland's most memorable moments in recent years, Robertson now stands on the brink of claiming a place in history all of his own.

A record that has stood for four decades is within touching distance, and few would begrudge him the opportunity to make it his own.

#1958. Wigan Athletic boss Gary Caldwell expecting ‘even more aggressive’ Barnsley FC

Wigan Athletic boss Gary Caldwell is expecting Barnsley to be even more aggressive than they were when the sides last met in August.

Before a ball had been kicked in League One, the sides played out a 1-1 draw at Oakwell in the Carabao Cup. Barnsley emerged victorious on penalties, with the since-departed Josh Earl steering home the winning spot-kick.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

The cup tie gave Wigan an insight into Barnsley’s high-octane approach and Caldwell is anticipating even more intensity when the sides meet in the league tomorrow (November 14).

He told Wigan’s YouTube channel: “I don’t think it’s an easy game by any stretch. I think they’re a really aggressive team. They make it very difficult for you when you’re in possession, we’ve seen in the first game this season, when we played against them in the cup.

“They’re a difficult team to beat, even though I felt we beat them on that day with the two perfectly good goals that we scored. It was still a really difficult game and it will be again on Saturday.

“If anything I think they’re even more aggressive. I think they’re better at doing what they do. They want to press, they want to press with a real intensity and numbers and make it difficult, in a man-to-man type game. I think they’re even better at that than when we first played them. We know it’s a really tough game, but it’s a game at home.”

Wigan and Barnsley sit 21st and 23rd respectively in the League One table but both have shown signs of life in recent weeks.

The Latics defeated Crewe Alexandra in the EFL Trophy earlier in the week, while the Reds swept Oldham Athletic aside in the same competition.

Caldwell said: “We’re in probably as good a place as we’ve been all season. A lot of things are starting to come together. The biggest thing I said after Tuesday night, winning football matches is a habit, a very good habit to get into. Having gone behind again, which is disappointing, to come back again, another good habit to have.

“So many things in the team are starting to come together. Now we need consistency of behaviours, consistency of performance, which will lead to consistency of results to keep building on what we’ve been doing in recent games.

“I think it’s a positive we’re at home. I think we’ve been very good at home this season and recently that has shown in the results.”

#1957. Rangers player red carded on international duty as horror tackle sparks VAR intervention

Rangers midfielder Vanja Dragojević was one of two Serbia players sent off in their 3-1 defeat by Germany on Friday night.

The 20-year-old received his marching orders following a VAR intervention after coming on as a substitute at half-time in the Nations League encounter in Belgrade.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Dragojević has found first-team opportunities hard to come by at Ibrox this season following his summer move from Partizan Belgrade. He has made just four starts across all competitions, and has been an unused substitute in 10 of the 12 matches played in the Scottish Premiership thus far.

Dragojević was also named on the bench for Serbia but was introduced at the break with his team losing 2-0 to win his third cap.

The scoreline was 3-1 to the visitors when the Rangers man caught Germany captain Joshua Kimmich on the ankle with a late tackle in the 76th minute. Replays showed Kimmich's ankle twist under the impact, though he avoided a serious injury.

Spanish referee Javier Alberola Rojas initially issued a yellow card for the foul but following a Video Assistant Referee (VAR) check and a pitchside monitor review, the punishment was upgraded to a straight red card.

Dragojević's dismissal halted Serbia's second-half momentum after they had pulled a goal back. Fellow substitute Andrija Živković was later sent off in the 89th minute for a second bookable offence, leaving the Serbians to finish the match with nine players.

Before his dismissal, Dragojević completed seven of his nine passes, made one clearance, and won one tackle. He is now suspended for Serbia's final Nations League group match away to Greece on Monday.

A straight red card carries an automatic minimum one-match international suspension, which could be extended by UEFA's disciplinary body for serious foul play

#1956. England's Harry Kane wants his next Wembley trophy to be in the Euro 2028 final

Thursday was Kane's night at England's spiritual home as he made a goal then scored his 92nd for his country on the occasion of his record-breaking 126th cap for the Three Lions.

But it was also an opportunity to mark him becoming the first Englishman since Michael Owen in 2001 to win the Ballon d'Or – the annual prize for the best European-based footballer and de facto, best player in the world.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Kane received it at a ceremony in London last month, and was presented with it before his club Bayern Munich's game against Borussia Dortmund, but it was important to him to do it again on international duty.

And it made him dream of captaining England to a first major trophy since 1966 when the European Championship final returns to Wembley in 2028.

"I think the crowd would be a bit more crazy if we're lifting the Euro 2028 trophy, that's for sure," said Kane. "But it inspired me.

"To be able to share the Ballon d'Or with our fans is important because we haven't won it for a long time.

"Not just the 126 (caps), but also the Ballon d'Or is an important occasion to mark.

"I know if we win a major tournament, which is my ultimate goal in my career, with England, then the celebration, not just in the stadium, but around the whole country, will be especially beautiful with it.

"I don't think I need any more motivation to make it happen, but it'll be incredible if we can."

Kane admitted on Thursday the enormity of what he has achieved this season has not yet hit him.

"The reception that I've had has been overwhelming and incredible," he said.

"I don't know if any of this has sunk in yet. Maybe in the (Bundesliga's) winter break, when I've got a couple of weeks off, I'll go on a beach somewhere and try and reflect on everything.

"Whether I'll be able to do that through my career, I'm not so sure. I'm so focused on just the next thing and the next moment.

"So if I've fully taken everything that I've achieved these last couple of weeks, I'm not quite sure. Ultimately, it's about the next thing. It's about Sunday (when England play Spain in a game to decide who tops their Nations League group), then it's about club football again.

"Hopefully over the Christmas break I'll have a good drink with my wife and take it all in."

#1955. Why England's Thomas Tuchel is right to talk up Spain 'final'

In reality, it is nothing of the sort. All that will be at stake at kick-off in the Metropolitano Stadium at 7.45pm is who wins Nations League A Group 3, and gets a home second leg in March's quarter-finals, but it makes sense for the coach to big it up.

Because if anything, England find matches between tournaments too easy. They qualified for the last World Cup without conceding a goal, yet found it hard work in America and Mexico.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

The Nations League is supposed to match equals, yet they ran out 7-0 winners in Croatia in October. That Thursday's 2-1 win in the reverse game was much tighter was cause for celebration with Tuchel.

"Because we didn't take our chances it was a tight match, which is good overall," he reflected, “because it can't always be glamorous and super-exciting. Sometimes it's about being serious and determined.

"We wanted a final, and on Sunday in Spain we have it."

Tuchel might rest the man he says is still his first-choice goalkeeper, Jordan Pickford, to give Leeds United's James Trafford another chance, slightly undermining his billing of the game.

But Trafford is getting his chance because he is performing so well and other changes will be more likely to strengthen England, with Ezri Konsa and Djed Spence likely to be available after injury and Miles Lewis-Skelly having served a one-match ban.

The narrative around this generation of England players is that they are flat-track bullies, brilliant in qualifying but flaky in finals and semi-finals, or whenever they come up against the world's elite.

World and European champions Spain won 3-2 at Wembley in September, so only need a draw.

They beat England in the last European Championship final, the second in a row the Three Lions had been tamed in. They lost this year's World Cup semi-final to Argentina and started the nearly-men cycle with a last-four defeat to Croatia in 2018.

When they got to the Nations League semi-finals in 2019, poor defending by John Stones and Kyle Walker saw them lose 3-1 to the Netherlands in extra-time.

So no, Sunday is not a "final", a huge occasion, a do-or-die moment for Tuchel's team. But it will not do them any harm to think so.

#1954. Scotland set to face much-changed team as Switzerland boss sets out ‘less serious’ final game plans

Scotland will face a heavily rotated team when they meet Switzerland in their final Nations League group game on Monday, with head coach Murat Yakin admitting he will look to rest several stars.

The 0-0 draw against Slovenia on Friday night confirmed Switzerland’s place as Group B1 winners on 13 points, meaning they’ll be promoted to League A regardless of Monday's result in St Gallen. However, it is a must-win for Scotland if they want to qualify for the promotion playoffs.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Currently third in the group, Sebastien Pocognoli’s team are one point behind Slovenia going into their final group game. To progress to a playoff, they must hope North Macedonia pull off a result against Slovenia in Skopje, while they must also beat Switzerland.

“I was actually a little surprised,” said Yakin after Friday night’s goalless draw. “For them [Slovenia], it was really an all-or-nothing game. But I wasn’t unhappy that they didn’t throw everything forward in the end. I’m relieved that we earned the points we needed. The expectations and pressure were enormous, but we showed a lot of maturity.

“If we convert one of the few chances we had, we win the game. But it's okay like this, too. We put ourselves in a good starting position, and we played it out calmly. It was a mature team performance We knew we were playing against a strong team with a good transition game. It was anything but easy. At times, there were ten players in their own penalty area. The opponent didn't allow much. Slovenia is very tough, well-organized, and sits very deep. We had to be careful there [against counterattacks]. We can be happy and proud.”

However, after securing the result they needed in Maribor, the 52-year-old conceded his side wouldn’t need to take the game as seriously against Scotland, explaining they will use the game as an opportunity to give some fringe squad members a chance to impress ahead of the upcoming European Championship 2028 qualifiers, which begin in March.

Already without experienced captain Granit Xhaka due to a calf injury, the Swiss media believe Borussia Dortmund goalkeeper Gregor Kobel is likely to be rested, with one of Silas Huber, Yvon Mvogo or Marvin Keller deputising. Elsewhere, uncapped squad members such as Samuel Ballet and Roggerio Nyakossi could be given their international debuts when Scotland come to town on Monday.

“We do need the necessary stability and seriousness,” admitted Yakin. “But we’ll definitely make a few changes. There are another three or four guys that I would like to see from the start. Monday is about prestige, points, and putting on a good show for our own fans. There were discussions with the clubs that one or two players would be rested once promotion was secured—but I'm not going to replace the entire team.”

#1953. HEARTS 2 FALKIRK 5: Wouter Vrancken slams 'childish' Hearts as five-star Bairns toy with injury-hit capital men at Tynecastle

Published: 16:57 EST, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 17:00 EST, 8 November 2026

Wouter Vrancken condemned a ‘ridiculous’ first-half display from his sorry Hearts side as their 18-month unbeaten home record in the Premiership was ripped apart by ruthless Falkirk.

The beleaguered Tynecastle side, who went into the game without 11 players through injury following a gruelling run of fixtures, endured a dismal afternoon as the Bairns raced into a 4-0 half-time lead on their way to a fifth Premiership win in a row.

Finley Barbrook, Owen Eames, Liam Henderson and Jacob Murrell’s double had the visitors 5-0 up within 47 minutes before Hearts reduced the deficit through substitute Sabri Guendouz and a Claudio Braga penalty.

It was a first league defeat at Tynecastle since April 2025 for the Gorgie men, who have now won just two of their last 11 matches in all competitions.

‘This is an embarrassment, the first half for sure,’ said Vrancken. ‘Always doubting, always doing things half-half, in possession, out of possession, everything, and such easy goals again.

‘When you give those easy goals, then you cannot win a game. It’s childish goals and cannot happen on this level. Those simple things, they are the basics actually in these situations.

American striker Jacob Murrell races off to celebrate his side's fifth goal on a day to remember

‘It’s crazy, crazy, and everybody — me, staff, players — have to take responsibility in those things. This is ridiculous.’

To exacerbate their grim predicament, Hearts lost yet another senior player as defender Malachi Fagan-Walcott limped off in the second half.

‘This also makes me a bit angry, because now we lose Mal again,’ said Vrancken. ‘Hopefully it’s not too bad, but still we had to replace him there, because he was one of the guys who was good in the game and in the last games actually he had a really consistent, good level.’

Hearts were leapfrogged into third place by Falkirk, who secured five consecutive top-flight victories for the first time in 31 years.

‘I’ve never been 5-0 up here before,’ said Bairns manager John McGlynn. ‘First half we were outstanding. A great start to the game for us to get the goal so early.

‘We got ourselves 4-0 up at half-time, which is dreamland. Hearts had a lot of the ball and dominated the second period, but we’re taking 5-2 every day of the week, make no mistake about it.’

Wouter Vrancken has been beset by injury concerns but he was in no mood for excuses

The Bairns seized the lead in the fourth minute. After Murrell’s close-range effort from Scott Tanser’s cross was brilliantly saved by Beau Reus, Barbrook reacted quickest to drill home a low, angled finish from eight yards out.

Falkirk doubled their lead in the 17th minute after the hosts were caught wide open on the counter-attack. Yan Dhanda’s shot from distance was charged down, allowing the Bairns to break swiftly, with Brad Spencer weighting his pass perfectly for Eames who fired past the exposed Reus.

Braga thought he had pulled one back for Hearts in the 20th minute, but it was ruled out for handball.

Falkirk took full advantage of this reprieve by adding a third in the 33rd minute as Murrell peeled off Fagan-Walcott at the back post to nod home Deniss Melniks’ cross from the right.

The visitors struck again in first-half stoppage-time as Henderson curled high past Reus after Tanser’s corner broke to him just inside the box.

Within two minutes of the restart Falkirk notched again as Murrell fired home after being set up by Ethan Ross.

Former Hearts boss John McGlynn led his side to a quite remarkable fifth consecutive win

Hearts got off the mark when Guendouz drilled in his first goal for the club from just inside the box in the 50th minute. Braga then tucked away a penalty in the 74th minute after Guendouz was tripped by Lewis Neilson, but it was far too little, far too late.

McGlynn added: ‘We had to smell blood and we had to go for it and that’s exactly what happened. Our play was outstanding in the first half. We won every duel, we won everything all over the park.

‘Winning five on the trot has not been done since 1995, Jim Jefferies’ team, so I’m delighted for everyone at the football club that we’ve managed to equal that record.’

#1950. Harry Kane on the inspiration to keep on shining for England

Thursday night at Wembley was not about England v Croatia, not really. It was not particularly about the Nations League, where the hosts needed to avoid a seven-goal defeat to be sure of going through to the quarter-finals (ooh the jeopardy!). It was all about Kane.

England's captain was greeted with a huge tifo as he led his team out of the tunnel for the 98th time.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Before the anthems and handshakes he broke from the line to pick his Ballon d'Or trophy off a plinth, and be presented with a framed shirt to mark his 126th appearance for the Three Lions, a new record.

Luka Modric handed him a replica of Croatia's oldest preserved football, brought to Zupanja by English industrialists in 1880.

It was a nice touch between two teams who have got to know each other rather well in the 21st Century, and two players who were team-mates at Tottenham Hotspur.

Modric is 41 years-old, eight years his senior. When he was 33, Modric also won the Ballon d'Or but it has not sated his appetite.

He was only a substitute when he won his 207th Croatia cap on Thursday, but it was telling he was given a warm ovation when he came off the bench in the second half with the game still in the balance.

Few opposing players get that at Wembley, and it was in stark contrast to the reception afforded to former Leeds United loanee Ben White when he came off the home bench two minutes later. He has not been forgiven for abandoning the ship at the 2022 winter World Cup.

Modric plays his club football at AC Milan, where there is a proud history of elderly players thriving, and has contributed nearly 750 Serie A minutes already this season.

Kane seems to be getting better, a more rounded player with every year of his 30s.

His part in the first goal was a case in point. The younger Kane did not often drop deep and play passes of the quality that released Jude Bellingham to set up Morgan Rogers for England's opener in the 2-1 win, but the 2026 version spends more time away from the frontline than on it.

"That's an area of the pitch I like to play in, that kind of left pocket," he explained. "The more I play with the guys, the more of a relationship I build up with Jude and Morgan and Trent (Alexander-Arnold, selected at right-back), whoever's playing, they know when I'm in that position, I'm probably going to play that type of ball, so they make the runs.

"It's just a pass that's a big strength of mine. It's something I've practised a lot when I was young and still do. You've seen over recent years, especially, that it's been a big weapon."

To carry on as long as Modric is a big ask but Kane has plenty of incentive to go on a couple more years yet.

His penalty to win the game five minutes after sloppy England set-piece defending brought Croatia back into it with a Petar Sucic strike was his 92nd goal for his country.

Only three other players – Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Iran's Ali Daei – have hit 100 in international football but there was no dodging the question when he was asked if it was possible: "I think it's achievable for sure."

And with the talent around him, leading his team onto the winner's podium at the 2028 European Championship final at Wembley, after consecutive losing finals, looks realistic too.

"If we win a major tournament, which is my ultimate goal, the celebrations not just inside the stadium, will be incredible," he said.

Seeing someone like you achieve what you want to is perhaps the biggest motivation of all.

"He's an inspiration for all of us," marvelled Kane when asked about Modric. "What an incredible player, what a great person as well, and someone who's looked after himself, a great professional.

"To be playing at 41 now, still at this level, is a credit to all of his hard work and his mentality. That inspires me to push to the limits.

"I think you just keep going to see how far your body takes you, your mentality takes you.

"As long as I feel like I can help the national team, as long as I feel like I'm performing at the highest level, I'll be here. Whether that's until I'm 40 we'll have to wait and see.

Thursday was just about celebrating one of the England greats and having failed to score and even missed a penalty since being crowned European football’s best player, he did not disappoint.

"It's demanding to get all the recognition, all the prizes, all the acknowledgement,” said Kane’s coach, Thomas Tuchel. “The gentleman he is, he responds to everything.

"It would be easy to lose focus, which he obviously never does.

"We were determined to get this result on his special evening. That he got it in the end with a decisive penalty makes it even more perfect.”

England won 7-0 in Croatia in October. Kane made Thursday top it.

#1948. Hibs struggler’s difficult start addressed as major doubts cast on wisdom of Easter Road transfer

Hibs striker Nathan Lowe’s has been told his early-season struggles at the club evidence the gulf in quality between the Scottish Premiership and the English second tier.

Lowe, 21, joined the club on a season-long loan from Stoke City in the summer, but has struggled to make an impact at Easter Road, scoring just twice in all competitions. Mirroring his difficult loan spells at Wycombe Wanderers and Stockport County last season, sections of the Hibs support are far from convinced by the imposing forward.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

However, former Stoke and Reading striker Dave Kitson believes his difficulties in the capital are in part due to a major difference in style and standard with the EFL Championship, with the 46-year-old questioning whether Lowe’s decision to move to Hibs was a wise one.

“Going up to Scotland was never going to be easy [for Lowe],” said Kitson. “It's two completely different styles of football. Scottish football to English Championship football is night and day. The Championship at the moment is unbelievably competitive. Virtually the whole league has been in the Premier League at some point and come down.

“Twenty years ago, paying £3 million for a striker was a lot. Now £30 million doesn't make anyone bat an eyelid. It's so competitive, which is why culture can be a real difference maker. You can't turn up anywhere, like away at Millwall, and just assume you're going to win. Any team can beat anyone on their day. It's so much harder than it used to be.”

The 21-year-old scored 18 goals in the 2024/25 season for EFL League Two club Walsall, and declared he intended to end the season as the league’s top scorer, saying: “I am by no means am I the finished article and I won't be at the end of this loan. But every season I go into, my aim is to be the top goalscorer in the league. Hopefully I can add to my tally significantly here.”

However, Lowe has scored just one league goal for Hibs this season, and his progress has now been stalled further due to injury. He hasn’t played for the club since the 1-0 defeat to Dundee United on October 10 because of a stress fracture.

Head coach Marink Reedijk revealed earlier this week that he expects to be without his services for an indefinite period and, with his loan spell not going to plan so far, former Stoke favourite Kitson believes he will be experiencing a dose of reality after his ambitious pre-season claims.

“Signing for Celtic or Rangers wasn't really an option for me,” Kitson told Lyllo Casino. “But thinking back, when you look at Celtic and Rangers back then, they had players like Henrik Larsson and Chris Sutton and before that Brian Laudrup, and Paul Gascoigne. That was proper quality. It's hard for them up there now because there isn't Premier League money. It's a tough league to go and prove yourself, especially if you're a young kid going on loan thinking you're going to rip up trees. That path is really difficult to tread these days.”

#1947. 'I have a letter from a nine-year-old fan on my cupboard door' - Sheffield United's Amy Andrews motivated by taking unconventional route

There is no lip service being paid, on whatever side of the barrier you stand. Amy Andrews was one of those girls who leant across in her youth, now it is she who makes a few memories for the smiling faces of the young Sheffield United fans that greet her at Bramall Lane.

“You don't realise who's there waiting for you, there could be a child that's been waiting for so long to meet you and for you to just sign something and have a photo with them and it means the world,” says the 26-year-old forward who is in her second year with the Blades in WSL2.

“We have the opportunity to give back to our fans that spend money and time coming to watch us. We get letters from the fans. I had one from a nine-year-old that I've stuck on my cupboard door. I look at it every day and it motivates me.”

Her own story is an inspirational one. Andrews didn’t get into professional football via the now conventional route through an elite club academy.

She had to go to America to find her path after two club academies near her Birmingham home chewed her up and spat her out.

“I felt like we weren't really cared for,” laments Andrews. “It made me quit the game for a year and then I went back to my local club with my best friends because I just wanted to enjoy my football again.

“Then America came up and that's how I got here, I had to take the harder route, I've been fighting against opinions and a different background all my life.

“There's kids now that have got Nike deals who are assigned to WSL teams but haven't played in the WSL.

“Going to America (she attended Western Illinois) shaped me to be the player and person I am today, because you just learn so much, leaving home at 18. It was quite difficult at first but I got used to it in the end, and I'd do it again if I could and would definitely recommend it.”

When she returned home she had spells in the second tier with Durham Cestria and Newcastle United. But after falling out of favour at Newcastle when new investment came in, Sheffield United offered her a fresh start in July 2025.

“When I met with the coaching staff and analysts, they valued me a lot, they showed me clips of me playing and how they're going to bring that out of me,” says Andrews.

“I just thought I need to get a hard-working club that's going to play me and value me.”

She has found her home in Sheffield. Andrews scored 10 goals last season - “United helped me rediscover my confidence” - and bagged her first hat-trick against former club Durham at Bramall Lane in September.

“That’s something I’ve had on my list of goals since I've turned professional, so it meant a lot,” she beams. “But I immediately turned my thoughts to when can I get my next one.”

It may happen on Saturday night against Bristol City at Bramall Lane, a showcase game for which adult tickets are £10, concessions £5.

“The pitch at Bramall Lane is so smooth, like a carpet,” she says.

“It's a privilege to play there. I remember playing for Newcastle at St James’ Park against AC Milan, scoring the equaliser in the last minute and then a penalty in the penalty shoot-out; that was unbelievable. I played there when there were 38,000 fans - amazing

“It gave me a taster of what I want to achieve. I know I'm good enough to get to the WSL. There's no point playing football if you don't have those goals, because what are you fighting for?

“I never got that opportunity to take the conventional route when I was growing up, so that's what I'm striving for. That's what motivates me.

“I feel like the odd one out. I'm so hungry to prove people wrong. I want people to hear my story.
